claims.text: In-situ laser remelting immediately after initial layer deposition will produce a more homogeneous AlCrFeNiSi microstructure than LPBF without remelting.
In-situ laser remelting will minimize elemental segregation in additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi.
In-situ laser remelting will reduce residual thermal stresses in additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi.
The reductions in segregation and residual stress will improve the overall mechanical integrity of AlCrFeNiSi.
Conventional processing and additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi entail risks of compositional segregation and residual thermal stress.
The proposed intervention is a secondary in-situ laser-remelting pass immediately after initial LPBF layer deposition.
An adequately tuned remelting pass can induce melt-pool mixing without excessive overheating or evaporation.
The intervention is valid within an unspecified LPBF processing window typically used for high-entropy alloys.
Laser remelting will refine and homogenize the microstructure.
Laser remelting will reduce elemental segregation at grain and melt-pool boundaries.
The secondary laser-remelting pass enhances melt-pool convection.
The secondary laser-remelting pass induces rapid resolidification.
Enhanced convection and rapid resolidification promote elemental mixing and recrystallization.
Microstructural homogenization alleviates microsegregation and residual stresses arising from thermal gradients.
Remelted AlCrFeNiSi specimens will have greater tensile strength and ductility than specimens produced by LPBF without remelting.
Remelted AlCrFeNiSi specimens will have lower porosity and microcrack density than specimens produced by LPBF without remelting.
Conventional LPBF of AlCrFeNiSi without remelting typically produces significant segregation, residual thermal stress, and processing defects.
The beneficial effect may fail when laser control or thermal management is insufficiently precise or when remelting causes detrimental overheating.
